title: 春望
author: Du Fu

translation: The state is broken, yet hills and rivers remain
Spring in the city: grass and trees grow wild
Grieved by the times, even flowers shed tears
Pained by parting, even birds startle the heart
Beacon fires have burned for three months straight
A letter from home is worth ten thousand gold
My white hair, scratched at, grows ever thinner
Soon it won't even hold a hairpin

annotations.国破: the state is broken — written during the An Lushan Rebellion, after the capital fell
annotations.溅泪: to splash tears — flowers seem to weep, or the poet weeps at flowers; both readings coexist
annotations.烽火: beacon fires — the ancient alarm system, here meaning continuous war
annotations.抵: to be worth, to equal in value
annotations.搔: sāo — to scratch (one's head, in worry)
annotations.浑欲不胜簪: almost unable to hold a hairpin — hair so thin from anxiety it can't be pinned up

appreciation: Du Fu's most devastating poem, written in the occupied capital Chang'an during the An Lushan Rebellion. Spring still arrives — but nature's indifference makes the ruin worse: the state is broken, 'yet hills and rivers remain.' The horror is domestic too: in wartime, a single letter from home outvalues gold. Eight lines, forty characters, and the whole sorrow of a civilization.
